significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish the form-(iii) law that the behavioral cost of ablating a language-localized circuit increases with non-linguistic structural depth—its predicted "depth-by-ablation interaction"—alongside the form-(ii) mechanism that the same components causally support linguistic parsing, arithmetic, logic, parentheses, and code. This would fix expectations across several task families and support a shared-substrate explanation of language and structured reasoning; Mahowald et al., "Dissociating language and thought in large language models: a cognitive perspective" (Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 2024), identifies precisely this separation between linguistic and broader cognitive competence as consequential, while the claim supplies a component-level causal answer rather than a mere performance correlation. Verified false is also determinate and informative: a syntax-selective circuit showing no depth-selective effect outside language would support the quoted "structure engine is domain-specific" conclusion, although the inference remains bounded to the stated open-weight-model case study. Topic substitution fails: merely restating "the relationship between language and AI intelligence" would not earn this score; the cross-domain depth law, causal circuit reuse, and converse transfer are specific additions beyond the topic-median hypothesis.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "rank-ordered component set S_syn," the "accuracy-vs-depth ablation curves," and the proposed ability to "probe or steer reasoning via the shared syntax circuit." Steering can act ex ante or during inference before a nested-reasoning answer is produced, whereas the ablation curve and circuit-overlap measure are primarily post-hoc diagnostics rather than advance failure forecasts. After per-model re-extraction, the conclusion predicts a transferable relation—deeper non-linguistic nesting should produce a steeper S_syn-specific ablation cost—not merely a procedure for searching, but its asserted scope is only "several open-weight models," with frontier-model generalization explicitly left open; likely downstream users therefore include interpretability researchers and model auditors, with more tentative practitioner uptake. Topic substitution again fails: the broad language–intelligence topic supplies neither these handles nor the transferable depth relation, so the reach score comes from the claim-specific conclusion.
